# A cloud-native store: Copernicus Marine {#sec-cmems}

```{r}
#| include: false
source("R/book.R")
```

Copernicus Marine publishes its gridded products as Zarr V2 on public
object storage, and publishes each one twice. The *timeChunked* copy has
chunks shaped like maps: one day of global sea level is nine chunks of
1024 x 512 cells. The *geoChunked* copy has chunks shaped like time
series: 33 years at one cell is six chunks of 16 x 8 cells by 2264 days.
The publisher has already done the work of making both kinds of read
cheap.

With [zaro](https://hypertidy.github.io/zaro/), either copy opens as a
lazy R array, unpacked to metres with missing values as `NA`:

```r
ds  <- zaro_dataset(zaro("https://s3.waw3-1.cloudferro.com/.../timeChunked.zarr"))
sla <- zaro_array(ds, "sla", cf = TRUE)
dim(sla)
#> [1]  2880  1440 12188
map <- sla[, , 12188]          # the latest day
```

That last line is the natural thing to write, and it is the read the
store was chunked for. On stock R it is 4.1 million element calls and
nine separate requests, one after another. The same goes for the series
`sla[i, j, ]` on the other copy.

## The reads

Five reads: a global map, a regional block of two weeks, and a full
series at one cell from the sea level product; then, from the global
waves product (3-hourly since 1980, chunks of 4 x 8 cells by 17,720
steps), 46 years at one cell and a year in a small box.

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| eval: false
#| file: scripts/03-cmems.R
```

```{r}
res <- book_run("03-cmems.R", live = TRUE)
book_table(res)
```

What to look for:

- **Requests** are equal in the two builds, or close to it, and so are
  the megabytes. Nobody is reading more or less data.
- **Fetch calls** drop to one. That one call carries every chunk, and
  zaro sends them through a single pool of 8 connections.
- The gain grows with the number of chunks in the read, up to the
  connection cap. Nine chunks cannot be more than nine times faster.
  The regional block, with a few dozen chunks, is where the batch earns
  the most.
- Decoding still happens in R, chunk by chunk, in both builds. That part
  of the time does not move.

```{r}
book_elt(res)
```

## The layout is the publisher's; the plan should be R's

The two copies exist because no single chunk shape serves maps and series
both. Choosing the copy is the user's one decision. After that, which
chunks to fetch and how to fetch them together is arithmetic on the
subscripts, and R has the subscripts. On stock R that arithmetic is
thrown away at the last step.

The connection cap matters as much as the plan once the plan exists.
Against this endpoint, 16 connections were about 1.5 times faster than 8
for a 268-chunk read, and 32 about 2 times (measured 2026-11-16). Set
`BOOK_MAX_CON` to try it; the default stays at a polite 8.
